feature.title: The edicts in stone
feature.lead: Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks, cave walls and tall polished pillars from Afghanistan to south India, in several languages and scripts. Here is where some of them still stand.

items.label: Kandahar Bilingual Rock
items.text: One of his earliest messages, written in Greek and Aramaic so the local people could read it. It praises piety and holding back from killing animals. It was found under rubble in 1958.

items.label: Maski Minor Rock Edict
items.text: Found by a mining engineer in 1915. It was the first edict found that names the king as Asoka, which proved that the edicts signed 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' were his.

items.label: Girnar
items.text: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts on one large boulder, in Brahmi script. Centuries later, around 150 AD, the ruler Rudradaman I added his own Sanskrit inscription to the same rock.

items.label: Kalsi
items.text: A full set of the fourteen Major Rock Edicts in Brahmi script.

items.label: Shahbazgarhi
items.text: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts in the Kharosthi script of the northwest. Vincent Smith translated Rock Edict 13, about Kalinga, from this text, which he called practically perfect.

items.label: Mansehra
items.text: Another full set of the fourteen Major Rock Edicts in Kharosthi script, carved on boulders.

items.label: Dhauli
items.text: Near the presumed site of the Kalinga war. The rock has Edicts 1 to 10 and 14, plus two special edicts for Kalinga in place of Edicts 11 to 13. Its front is carved as an elephant. A peace pagoda was built on the hill in 1972.

items.label: Jaugada
items.text: The second copy of the special Kalinga edicts. Here Ashoka tells his officials: 'All men are my children.'

items.label: Yerragudi
items.place: near Gooty, Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, (India)
items.text: All fourteen Major Rock Edicts plus two Minor Rock Edicts, spread over six boulders in the Yenakonda hills.

items.label: Sopara
items.text: Only fragments of Edicts 8 and 9 survive, on a free-standing stone near the old western seaport.

items.label: Barabar Caves
items.text: Caves cut into hard granite and given to the Ajivikas, a group of ascetics who were not Buddhist, in his 12th and 19th years. Someone later chiselled at the word 'Ajivikas', but it can still be read.

items.label: Sarnath Lion Capital
items.place: Sarnath Museum, near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, (India)
items.text: Four lions back to back above wheels and four animals. It was dug up in 1905 and inspired the State Emblem of India and the wheel on India's flag.

items.label: Sanchi pillar
items.text: A polished pillar beside the Great Stupa, carrying an edict against splitting the Buddhist order. Its four-lion capital is in the Sanchi Archaeological Museum.

items.label: Lumbini pillar
items.text: Set up when Ashoka visited the Buddha's birthplace in his 20th year. It says 'the Buddha Sakyamuni was born here' and made the village free of taxes. It was rediscovered in 1896.

items.label: Delhi-Topra pillar
items.text: The only pillar with all seven Pillar Edicts. Sultan Firoz Shah Tughlaq moved it from Topra in 1356. James Prinsep read its Brahmi letters in 1837.

items.label: Allahabad pillar
items.text: First stood at Kausambi. It carries Pillar Edicts 1 to 6, the Queen's Edict, and the edict against splitting the Buddhist order.

items.label: Rampurva pillars
items.text: Two pillars, one topped by a lion and one by a bull. The lion pillar carries Pillar Edicts 1 to 6.

timeline.title: Born a Maurya prince
timeline.text: Ashoka was probably born in Pataliputra around 304 BC; the year is only an estimate. His father was Bindusara, the second Maurya emperor, and his grandfather was Chandragupta, who founded the empire. Sources give different names for his mother.

timeline.title: A prince in the provinces
timeline.text: The year is unknown. Later Buddhist texts say his father sent him to put down a revolt at Taxila, and the Sri Lankan chronicles say he governed Ujjain. An inscription records a visit he made as a prince, but scholars differ on how much of these stories is history.

timeline.title: Devi of Vidisha
timeline.text: Sri Lankan tradition says that on his way to Ujjain he met Devi, a merchant's daughter from Vidisha, near Sanchi. The same tradition names their children Mahinda and Sanghamitta. The date is unknown.

timeline.title: A contested throne
timeline.text: When Bindusara fell ill, Ashoka took control of the capital. Legends say he fought his half-brothers and killed 99 or 100 of them; modern historians call these numbers exaggerated, and one of his own edicts mentions his brothers' families. Vincent Smith dated his accession to about 273 BC; Wikipedia gives about 269 to 268 BC.

timeline.title: Legends of a cruel king
timeline.text: Later Buddhist stories call the young king 'Chandashoka' and tell of harsh punishments. Modern historians think these tales were made darker so that his later change would seem more wonderful.

timeline.title: Formally crowned
timeline.text: The Sri Lankan chronicles say he was consecrated about four years after taking power, which may point to a war of succession. His edicts count his years from this consecration.

timeline.title: The conquest of Kalinga
timeline.text: In the eighth year after his consecration, probably 261 BC, his armies conquered Kalinga, a rich kingdom on the east coast. His own Rock Edict 13 says 150,000 people were carried away, 100,000 were killed and many more died. Some historians think the numbers may be partly rhetoric.

timeline.title: Remorse and a new path
timeline.text: Ashoka later wrote that the suffering of Kalinga filled him with sorrow and regret, and that the only true conquest was conquest by dhamma, the moral law. He made no new wars of conquest. Historians think his turn to Buddhism was gradual; Sri Lankan sources even place his conversion before the war.

timeline.title: A message in Greek and Aramaic
timeline.text: Around his tenth year, a message on a rock near Kandahar announced his teaching of piety to Greek and Aramaic speakers, and said that hunters and fishermen had stopped killing.

timeline.title: Pilgrimage to the Bodhi Tree
timeline.text: Rock Edict 8 says that after his tenth year he went to Sambodhi, the place of the Buddha's awakening. Instead of royal hunting trips, he made journeys to meet people, give gifts and teach about dhamma.

timeline.title: The first edicts
timeline.text: His earliest Minor Rock Edicts appeared from about his eleventh year. In them he says he had been a lay Buddhist for over two and a half years without much effort, then for more than a year had worked hard at it.

timeline.title: Caves for another faith
timeline.text: In his twelfth year Ashoka gave caves cut into the granite of the Barabar Hills to the Ajivikas, ascetics who were rivals of the Buddhists. He gave another in his nineteenth year.

timeline.title: Fourteen edicts on the rocks
timeline.text: From about his twelfth and thirteenth years, the Major Rock Edicts were carved at sites from Girnar in the west to Dhauli in the east and Shahbazgarhi in the north. They ban some animal sacrifice, set up care for people and animals, and ask for respect between faiths.

timeline.title: Officers of dhamma
timeline.text: In his thirteenth year he created a new kind of official, the Dhamma Mahamatras. Their job was the welfare of the old, the sick, women, children and all religious groups, including Greeks and other peoples in the northwest.

timeline.title: Five Greek kings named
timeline.text: Rock Edict 13 says his conquest by dhamma had reached as far as the Greek king Antiochus and four more kings: Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander. Scholars still debate exactly which rulers some of these names mean.

timeline.title: Special edicts for Kalinga
timeline.text: In Kalinga itself, the edict about the war was left out. Instead, two special edicts told the local officials to see that justice was done, saying 'All men are my children.'

timeline.title: The Third Buddhist Council
timeline.text: Sri Lankan tradition says that in his seventeenth year the monk Moggaliputta Tissa led a council of monks at Pataliputra with Ashoka's support. Northern Indian sources do not mention it, so some scholars doubt it happened.

timeline.title: Mahinda sails to Sri Lanka
timeline.text: Sri Lankan tradition says missions went out in his eighteenth year, around 250 BC. His son Mahinda, now a monk, led the mission to Sri Lanka with four other elders.

timeline.title: Pillars and lions
timeline.text: Polished stone pillars, 12 to 15 metres tall, were raised at Buddhist sites and other places in the north. The most famous capital, four lions back to back, crowned the pillar at Sarnath, where the Buddha first taught.

timeline.title: Sanghamitta and the Bodhi sapling
timeline.text: In his nineteenth year, tradition says, his daughter Sanghamitta, a nun, went to Sri Lanka to found an order of nuns, carrying a sapling of the Bodhi Tree.

timeline.title: At the Buddha's birthplace
timeline.text: In his twentieth year Ashoka came in person to Lumbini. He set up a stone pillar saying that the Buddha was born there, and made the village free of taxes, paying only an eighth share of its produce.

timeline.title: The Pillar Edicts
timeline.text: In his 26th and 27th years he issued the Pillar Edicts, his last major set of messages. The seventh lists his public works: shade trees and mango groves on the roads, wells, rest houses and watering places. Exact dates differ by a few years between scholars.

timeline.title: Death of the emperor
timeline.text: Sri Lankan tradition places his death in his 37th year as king, around 232 BC. His birth year is only estimated, so his age of about 72 is also uncertain, and no reliable source gives the place.

timeline.title: The letters are read again
timeline.text: For centuries no one could read the Brahmi script. James Prinsep deciphered it and read the Delhi and Allahabad pillars, and records from Sri Lanka sent by George Turnour linked the king 'Piyadasi' to Ashoka.

timeline.title: His name in stone
timeline.text: A mining engineer found an edict at Maski that calls the king 'Devanampiya Asoka'. It proved that the edicts signed only with a title were really Ashoka's.

timeline.title: The lions on the seal
timeline.text: On the day India became a republic, it adopted a State Emblem based on the Lion Capital from Sarnath. The wheel from the same capital is at the centre of India's flag.

works.title: The fourteen Major Rock Edicts
works.text: Fourteen messages carved on rocks across the empire, on animal life, care for the sick, honest officials, respect between faiths and, in Edict 13, regret for the Kalinga war.

works.title: The Minor Rock Edicts
works.text: His earliest group of edicts, found mostly in central and south India. They describe his own growing effort as a Buddhist and urge 'small and great' to try.

works.title: The special Kalinga edicts
works.text: Two edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada, written for the conquered province. They tell the officials in Kalinga to see that justice is done to the people, because, Ashoka says, all men are his children.

works.title: The seven Pillar Edicts
works.text: Messages carved on tall polished pillars near the end of his reign, reviewing his work for dhamma and his public works.

works.title: The Kandahar Greek and Aramaic edict
works.text: A rare edict in Greek and Aramaic, showing he wrote for the languages his people actually used.

works.title: Care for people and animals
works.text: Rock Edict 2 describes medical care for people and for animals, with healing herbs, roots and fruits brought in and planted where they were missing.

works.title: Shade, wells and rest houses
works.text: Banyan trees and mango groves along the roads, wells, rest houses and watering places for travellers and animals.

works.title: Limits on killing animals
works.text: Rock Edict 1 says the royal kitchen, which once killed many animals a day, was cut to two peacocks and a deer, and that these too would stop.

works.title: Officers of dhamma
works.text: A new office, the Dhamma Mahamatras, to look after the welfare of the old, the sick, women, children and every religious group.

works.title: Officials on tour
works.text: Rock Edict 3 orders officials to tour their districts every five years to teach good conduct.

works.title: The Barabar cave gifts
works.text: Rock-cut caves given to the Ajivika ascetics, a faith other than his own.

works.title: The Lion Capital of Sarnath
works.text: A sandstone capital about 2.1 metres tall with four lions, now in the Sarnath Museum and the model for India's State Emblem.

works.title: The Great Stupa at Sanchi
works.text: Ashoka commissioned the first brick dome over relics of the Buddha at Sanchi. Later kings enlarged it and added the carved gateways. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

works.title: The Lumbini pillar
works.text: A pillar marking the Buddha's birthplace, with a short inscription about his visit and a tax cut for the village.

works.title: Missions abroad
works.text: According to Sri Lankan tradition, teachers were sent to other lands, with his son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta taking Buddhism to Sri Lanka.

books.title: Inscriptions of Asoka (Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, vol. 1)
books.author: Ashoka, edited and translated by E. Hultzsch
books.note: Ashoka's own words, as carved on rocks and pillars, in a careful scholarly translation (new edition, 1925).

books.title: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India (with the edicts)
books.author: Vincent A. Smith, with Ashoka's edicts translated by Smith
books.note: Second edition. Plain English versions of the edicts, plus a life story. Some of Smith's dates and views are now out of date.

books.title: Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas
books.author: Romila Thapar
books.note: The classic modern study of his reign and policy of dhamma (Oxford University Press; 3rd edition 2015).

books.title: Ashoka: The Search for India's Lost Emperor
books.author: Charles Allen
books.note: A lively account of how scholars rediscovered Ashoka through his inscriptions (The Overlook Press).

books.title: Ashoka in Ancient India
books.author: Nayanjot Lahiri
books.note: A modern life story by an archaeologist, built from the edicts and the places they stand (Harvard University Press).
